research_text:
# Research brief

## API and meaning of the finding

`java.security.KeyPairGenerator` creates public/private key pairs for a specified algorithm. The algorithm is selected by a static `getInstance` factory call; the generator can then be initialized and used to generate a pair. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))

In the supplied CrySL rule, the relevant value is **the first argument bound as `algorithm` in a `getInstance` event**. The reported message says the detector found `ED25519` where that rule permits only `RSA`, `EC`, `DSA`, `DiffieHellman`, or `DH`. It does not identify an invalid key size or establish that Java threw an exception. The exact analyzed call, provider, initialization and consumers were not supplied. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

Oracle documents `Ed25519` as a standard key-pair-generator algorithm for an Edwards-curve signature scheme, and its JDK 15 SunEC provider documentation lists an implementation. Thus, the rule’s exclusion is not a general Java API prohibition on Ed25519. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html

## Documented usage and remediation

- Obtain a generator for an algorithm supported by the selected provider. The provider may be selected explicitly, or Java can select one; an unavailable algorithm results in `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. Initialize with a provider-supported key size or algorithm-specific parameter specification, optionally supplying a `SecureRandom`, then generate a key pair. Unsupported sizes and inappropriate parameter specifications have documented exceptions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html?utm_source=openai))
- Java **permits generation without explicit initialization**: the provider supplies defaults. Oracle recommends explicit initialization because defaults can vary by provider and change between versions. For Ed25519, Java documents `NamedParameterSpec.ED25519`; the JDK 15 SunEC documentation also specifies a 255-bit default and restriction. These are provider/version-specific facts, not evidence of the arguments used in the reported finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
- Oracle’s recommendation concerning defaults is explicit initialization. The consulted API documentation does **not** prescribe replacing Ed25519 with one of this CrySL rule’s allowed algorithms as remediation for this finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/NamedParameterSpec.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/security/oracle-providers.html

## Compatibility and migration

- **Platform support:** Oracle documents SunEC support in JDK 15. Support on another runtime or provider must be established from that implementation’s documentation. Java SE 21’s mandatory-generator list does not include Ed25519, even though the standard-names specification lists it. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/security/oracle-providers.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Persisted and wire formats:** Java documents X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` and PKCS #8 `PrivateKeyInfo` encoded-key specifications. RFC 8410 specifies Ed25519’s algorithm identifier and its public-key, private-key and signature encodings. A shared container name alone does not establish that consumers support both its old and new algorithm contents. RFC 8410 also notes that some private-key importers do not accept a newer structure containing the public-key field. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/package-summary.html?utm_source=openai))
- The `KeyPairGenerator` API documentation consulted does **not** provide a migration procedure for existing persisted keys, certificates, signatures or peer protocols when changing algorithms. Compatibility therefore remains dependent on the actual formats, providers and consumers, none of which were supplied.

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/package-summary.html ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8410

## Exact published CrySL rule

The linked source is a moving `master` URL. It was consulted directly, but the supplied SHA-256 and the rule-pack commit used by the detector have **not been independently verified**.

The source’s factory-event matching clause and relevant constraint are: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPairGenerator
```

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;
```

```text
algorithm in {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"};
```

The same source declares `algorithm` as a `String`. Its event patterns constrain the factory call to one argument, or two arguments with the second represented by `_`. It also declares `initialize` patterns with one or two arguments, binding either an integer `keysize` or an `AlgorithmParameterSpec` `params`; and zero-argument `generateKeyPair` and `genKeyPair` events. The declared order is `Get, Init, Gen`. The rule additionally contains algorithm-dependent key-size constraints and `prepared…[params]` requirements. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

**A method on an unrelated type does not match merely because it shares one of these names:** the rule declares `java.security.KeyPairGenerator` as its `SPEC` and gives argument patterns. The rule text itself does not spell out all analyzer resolution details, including subtype handling or how a particular detector version handles an unbound `keysize` on a parameter-spec path; those remain unresolved without the analyzer version and trace. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl))

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPairGenerator.crysl
